fullText:
PlayStation 5 (version played), PC; Screen Burn
Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure

You spend a considerable portion of Silent Hill: Townfall in a kind of foetal position, cowering behind objects that will be eerily familiar to anyone who lived in the UK during the 1990s. Cars seem to be modelled on the era’s boxy Volkswagen Golfs; logos adorning phone boxes should narrowly escape the attention of copyright lawyers at BT Group. (For millennials, the deja vu will likely intensify the horror, as if stepping back into a childhood nightmare.) Simon, the nerdy, unassuming star of the game, pokes his head around corners to catch a glimpse of the demonic entities that wish to maim him, before shrinking back down again with a downwards motion of the analogue stick. In such moments, it’s easy to imagine him wrapping his arms around his knees, clasping his eyes shut and wishing himself away from this place.

The game’s setting, St Amelia, is based on the fishing communities of the East Neuk of Fife. The terror lurking here is wonderfully specific: absent lairds, island poverty, an oil-drilling corporation. Anguished beasts lumber down quaint streets lined with sandstone houses and fluttering bunting. This venerable horror series may have shifted to Scotland, yet we remain firmly in classic Silent Hill territory – weather and all. St Amelia finds itself suffused in supernatural fog and the vast majority of its inhabitants have vanished following some kind of mass tragedy. The artful, evocative presentation is such that you can almost taste the in-game air, the briny seaside tang diluted by rainy mist.

Visually, this scuzzy, grotty take on Silent Hill from Glasgow studio Screen Burn leans on bold juxtapositions of colour, shadow, and ominous silhouettes. Sometimes the stricken town is bathed in blood-red moonlight; often, pitch-black interiors are illuminated by harsh white torchlight. The arresting imagery brings to mind found-footage horror films such as Rec and the spine-tingling camcorder sections of UK classic, The Descent. Simon soon finds a portable television with strange, arcane power: it receives odd, elliptical messages from a nurse called Zoe, and tracks nearby monsters whose outline appears in scratchy low resolution on its small screen.

The action is slow-burning and absorbing: Simon lopes about town, hiding from depraved monsters and occasionally bludgeoning them to death with a pipe. To enter some buildings, he has to make an incision with a scalpel in a fleshy door opening as thick, fresh blood oozes out. Gradually, Simon’s reason for visiting St Amelia in the first place becomes clear: guilt. But he’s not the only one racked with it. Zoe, voiced with terrific glassy distance by Kezia Burrows, has her own hangups. The third playable character in this triple-threat portrait of shame and suffering is alpha male Richard, the CEO of an energy company that professed to bring prosperity to the island.

There were times when I was so locked in that the hours seemed to pass by in the blink of an eye, as if time had gone wonky just like in St Amelia. One memorable stretch takes place in a municipal-style high-rise building. Armed with a shotgun, and attempting to avoid the game’s nippiest, nastiest enemies, I ascended and descended each floor, as if playing a brutal, Ballardian take on The Raid. I have never felt such dread at the prospect of entering an open-plan office, knowing what lurked among mouldering office furniture and knackered desktop PCs.

Every element – scavenging for items, creeping between bins, running at full pelt when all else fails – pulls you deeper into Townfall. Its design broadly adheres to diegetic principles, in that most information is conveyed to you within the game: to view the map, for example, Simon physically pulls it out – the action never pauses. To save your progress, you must find a telephone in St Amelia, manually pick up the receiver, and then dial a number.

Puzzles function similarly. You snoop through emails, install floppy disks, and pocket important bits of paper, usually in an effort to gain a key code. These puzzles, though relayed via grounded, dated real-world tech, follow a serendipitous dream logic; even getting stuck feels coherent within the game’s uncanny psychogeographic claustrophobia. (That is, until it doesn’t. Close to the game’s conclusion, one esoteric puzzle about deciphering industrial symbols killed my progress, and my bafflement, frustration and rage had less to do with Townfall’s hallucinatory horror and more to do with its obtuseness.)

Not even a fiendishly illegible puzzle could derail Townfall. This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread. What’s most surprising is where the game’s sympathies lie: not with Simon, nurse Zoe, or bullyboy Richard, but the people of St Amelia. Their memorial in the centre of town is one of the game’s clearest images, unobscured by fog, though we’re never privy to the exact events that lead to their deaths. Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.

Silent Hill: Townfall is released 24 September; £44.99

title: ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100
description:
Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper
Apple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models.
It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rush hoovering up every memory chip available for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips, and other critical components, for electronics, including phones.
fullText:
Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper

Apple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models.

It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rush hoovering up every memory chip available for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips, and other critical components, for electronics, including phones.

The situation has dramatically driven up costs, with some chips five times dearer than previously listed. Therefore the everyday electronics products people rely on are suddenly significantly more expensive to make, and that is being passed on to consumers.

“Two things are happening at once,” says Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of client devices at research company IDC. “Component costs have risen sharply, with memory alone up more than 300% year on year.”

Because older iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones, Apple is pricing them as current products, he adds.

The iPhone is not the first product to have a “RAMageddon” price increase, but it is the single biggest-selling electrical product in the world. For many, this means the real cost of the AI splurge will be £100 without getting anything more for your money.

Other manufacturers of smartphones have also increased the price of new models, with Samsung and Google adding up to £80 to their flagship phones.

Apple has also increased the price of its refurbished stock by £60 to £70, including the older iPhone 15 that is no longer sold new in the shops. However, according to data from Uswitch, the increase in cost has yet to reach the third-party refurbished iPhone market.

“A refurbished iPhone 16 has held at about £503 all summer, roughly where it was before the 18 Pro launch,” says Ernest Doku, a Uswitch mobiles expert. “A refurbished 14 is about £10 cheaper than it was in June, while the 16 has simply stopped falling in price.”

Most smartphone makers, other than Apple, have discontinued older models that were no longer economically viable, and likely wouldn’t sell at higher prices. The impact has been particularly acute at the lower end of the market.

In its latest forecast, IDC predicts there will be the steepest annual contraction in worldwide smartphone sales on record this year, falling almost 17% to just over 1bn handsets. “People are buying fewer phones and paying considerably more for those they do buy,” Jeronimo says.

There have been bigger price rises for other electronics. Computer makers, which are much more exposed to rapidly jumping memory and chip costs, have had to raise prices several times over the past 18 months.

Microsoft added up to £220 to some of its Surface computers but also released versions with half as much memory as a way to attempt to keep prices down.

The move has forced the company to try to redesign Windows to run more comfortably with only 8GB of RAM, which it hasn’t for several years.

Many of PC maker Dell’s high-end laptops have jumped by as much as 25%, while the repairable laptop maker Framework has had to continually adjust prices as costs fluctuate.

Even Apple added £100 to its lower-cost MacBook Neo, as well as rises to most models in its Mac and iPad lines in June. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” the company says in a statement.

Games consoles aren’t immune, either. In a rare state of affairs, Microsoft recently increased the price of its near six-year-old console to £670, up from its original launch price of £449.

“Console storage and memory prices have increased by more than 2.5 times, and we expect another doubling by the autumn of 2027,” the company says.

Unfortunately, £100 added to the cost of a phone may only be the start of the price pain, with key memory producers, including SK Hynix, suggesting the shortages could last beyond 2030.

Jeronimo says memory prices are going to continue rising well into 2027, even if the pace has slowed from the “extraordinary spikes” seen earlier this year. “Even once memory costs ease, I do not expect smartphone prices to fall back to the same levels as last year.

“Increases in this industry tend to be sticky. Once customers have absorbed a higher price and manufacturers have rebuilt their margins, companies hold the line and add value through storage or features, rather than cutting the ticket price.”

The bad news for consumers is that “the era of cheap smartphones – or any device to be honest – is over,” Jeronimo says.

title: Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data
description:
Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests
Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones.
The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests

Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones.

The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took.

Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations had complained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy.

The DPC inquiry was prompted by research by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018 which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars).

The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data.

It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests.

“Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC.

“Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals.

“It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added.

Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”

The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, which claimed Google used “various tricks” to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled.

“Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council.

BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”.

Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”.

The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020.

Imposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months.

It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland.

It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m.

Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner.

“As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.

“The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle.

There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage.

title: Bears Keep Attacking My Garbage Bins, But the Flies Are Even Worse
description: Cleaning my garbage bins was a small project I kept putting off.
fullText:
The first time I saw 60 gallons of trash strewn across my lawn, I thought we'd been robbed. I recalled the last time I experienced a break-in: Shortly after college, at my dad's house in Detroit, burglars trashed our house and took the most random assortment of items, including my unopened college diplomas that had just arrived in the mail. But I wasn't in the city anymore; I was in the Catskill Mountains, home to about 2,000 bears.

I learned the hard way that once bears successfully raid your trash bin for food, they'll keep coming back. It highlighted another problem I had been ignoring: My trash bins reeked. I had never cleaned them since closing on our house, which invited a horde of flies, then bears that visited each week. A long-term solution might be bear-proof garbage cans or securing the lids with bungee cords, but I wanted to solve the simplest problem and clean my disgusting garbage bins.

My trash bins reeked in a way you can't imagine—or maybe you can, if you're like me and haven't cleaned them. If that's you, here's what I used to clean mine. And while you're here, I hope you follow along with my adventures as a first-time homeowner trying to make my house into the coolest house in the neighborhood. I invite you to follow along on our official Instagram, official YouTube, or my personal Instagram. I took care of the flies and bears, then installed permanent outdoor lights, then I'll build an outdoor fire pit—and that's just the beginning. I hope to see you along the way.

title: How to Claim Your Piece of Apple's $250 Million Siri Settlement
description: If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16, you may be eligible for a payout.
fullText:
Last week, Apple released Siri AI, the company's biggest overhaul to its smart assistant ever. If you have a compatible device running the latest updates, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, you now have access to Apple's AI-powered Siri, in addition to a number of new Apple Intelligence features. For some of us, this might seem like a welcome upgrade from a company that hasn't done as much with AI as its competitors. For others, it's a long overdue fulfillment of a promise. So overdue, in fact, that Apple may be offering a payout to make up for it.

This year's iOS updates aren't the first we've seen of Siri AI. Back in 2024, Apple advertised a new AI-powered Siri that could understand content on your screen and pull data from your various apps to inform its answers. In Apple's pre-recorded demos, for example, Siri could dive through your texts and emails to locate a family member's travel information if you asked the assistant what time that person's flight arrived. Apple said this new Siri would arrive with iOS 18 later that year, launching on compatible iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 devices. But while the company slowly rolled out Apple Intelligence features through the iOS 18 lifecycle, this new Siri was nowhere to be found.

For many, this absence ranged from mildly humorous to frustrating. Some, however, found it deceptive. After all, Apple said users who bought a certain iPhone could expect it to run this supercharged Siri. You might have picked up an iPhone 16, or perhaps the previous-generation iPhone 15 Pro, assuming you could take advantage of Apple's AI-powered assistant, but those changes didn't actually arrive until last week, more than two years after Apple first announced them. Depending on your upgrade cycle, you could be on your second or third smartphone since then.

These grievances weren't confined to grousing on the internet. The Clarkson law firm filed a suit against Apple, alleging the company misled customers with these new Siri features. While the company has not admitted wrongdoing, it did agree to a $250 million settlement to put the case aside. And if you're eligible, it is now time to claim your share of the settlement.

Not all iPhone owners are eligible for a slice of this settlement. Per the terms, only customers who bought an iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model (iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e) can claim a share. What's more, there's a specific timeline during which purchases are eligible: June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025.

If you bought your iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 between these dates, you can make a claim. To start, head to the settlement's official website, then choose "File A Claim." If you have a Claim ID and PIN, you can share them here. If you don't, you can still choose to file a claim online. You can share your iPhone's serial number, though if you don't have it, you can share your Apple Account email address and the number associated with your iPhone. Claims are open from today, Sept. 21, through Dec. 21.

While $250 million sounds like a huge payout, the final amount likely won't be: The estimated payout is $25 per claimant, though that may change depending on the number of respondents. If there are fewer claims than expected, you may receive as much as $95. As MacRumors reports, the final approval hearing is on Feb. 24 of next year, so don't expect the money any time soon.

title: The Best Gift Subscriptions for Every Type of Person
description: From learning to crafting to eating, these digital subscriptions are sure to please.
fullText:
The right subscription service for the right person is the ultimate "I see you" present, the kind of gift they'll appreciate every time they log into the news service you gave them, or every time the box with a tasty meal or cool gadget arrives on their porch. Below are the best gift subscriptions for every type of person, from the snobby cinephile to the terminally online.

Bespoke Post is my pick for the best overall because it solves that perpetual holiday problem of what to get the person who's impossible to shop for. Most gift box services are aimed at specific niches, but Bespoke Post casts a wider net by letting users choose exactly what comes in their box every month. One month they can get high-end coffee supplies. The next, outdoor gear. If nothing catches their eye, they can just skip a month. If you want to give someone a present they will truly never tire of, a subscription to Bespoke Post is for you.

If you're looking for a gift for someone who is constantly doomscrolling, get them a subscription to the New York Times. Its old-school, objective reporting is the antidote to social media alarmism, and it also has good recipes and the best puzzles. An all-access subscription opens up the full New York Times archive going back to 1851, NYT Cooking, daily crosswords, and the 10,000-puzzle archive (including Wordle, Connections, Spelling Bee, and all of your other favorite time-wasters).

If that person on your list is always trying to exercise their brain, a subscription to MasterClass is a lot cheaper than grad school. This educational streaming service covers a wide range of subjects, from science to acting to business, and includes extensive lectures from heavyweights in each field. They can take a deep dive into filmmaking with Martin Scorsese, take music lessons from Timbaland, or learn cooking from Gordon Ramsay. A subscription unlocks the entire library, so they can learn as much or as little as they choose.

Libro.fm lets users listen to audiobooks while supporting their local independent bookstore, instead of supporting a huge corporation that shall go unnamed. Libro's content is free of the digital rights management of its main competitor, so users can listen to the books they own however they like instead of being locked into a proprietary player. Libro's firm anti-AI-narration stance ensures you aren't paying for robotic readers, and users can choose which independent bookstore to support through Libro's profit-sharing model.

If you're buying a gift for someone who likes to make things with their hands, the Adults and Crafts crate will keep them busy with a monthly project to work on. Each crate includes the tools, materials, and instructions for a bespoke craft object—everything from pressed flowers to a resin fruit tray or an enamel glass painting. Not only will they end up with a unique object, but each project is also a mini-lesson in crafting techniques.

If someone you know is drowning in debt from paying for DoorDash and Uber Eats, get them a sub to CookUnity. It's not one of those services that delivers ingredients and instructions; CookUnity provides restaurant-quality meals created by star chefs like Esther Choi and Marcus Samuelsson for around $11 each, and the only "cooking" required is a little microwaving.

If you're buying a gift for a film lover who thinks The Criterion Channel is too mainstream, hit them with a membership to Eternal Family, a streaming service that bills itself as the "hidden gem video store." They don't mean "hidden gems" that are actually widely known, like The Prestige or something. This is the uncut stuff, like Heino Pars' achingly beautiful 1983 stop-motion film Valley of the Honey Makers (way better than Bee Movie) or In the Dust of the Stars, a visionary science fiction film made behind the Iron Curtain in Romania in 1976. Every option is a different strange delight you likely can't watch anywhere else.

title: Ex-Liverpool star Salah given six-month driving ban
description: The former Liverpool footballer's Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding in Wilmslow in March.
fullText:
Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.

Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents.

The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge.

He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court.

A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce.

The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team.

Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history".

He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season.

title: Swimming sensation Yu, 13, wins second Asian Games gold
description: Thirteen-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi continues her record-breaking exploits at the Asian Games by winning gold in the 200m individual medley.
fullText:
Thirteen-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi continued her record-breaking exploits at the Asian Games by winning gold in the 200m individual medley.

China's Yu won in a new Games record of two minutes 06.10 seconds in Tokyo and was just four-tenths of a second behind the world record.

"Very excited, very happy. It's an achievement that shows the hard work of our team," said Yu.

The schoolgirl also set an Asian Games record in winning the 200m butterfly to claim her first major gold on Sunday's opening day.

She added: "I'm happier with the second gold medal than the first."

Yu became the youngest swimmer to win a medal at the World Championships when she took bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China's 4x200m freestyle relay team last year.

title: Lions tour a 'top goal' for Wales prop Tuipulotu
description: Wales prop Sisilia Tuipulotu says selection for next year's inaugural British and Irish Lions women's tour is among her top rugby priorities.
fullText:
Wales prop Sisilia Tuipulotu says selection for next year's inaugural British and Irish Lions women's tour is among her top rugby priorities.

The in-form tight-head scored two tries in Wales' emphatic 50-19 victory over South Africa on Friday, under the watchful eye of Lions head coach Jo Yapp.

With Yapp saying she will only take the best players in each position, most of the touring party to New Zealand is expected to be made up of England's world cup-winning stars.

But Tuipulotu's barnstorming display certainly puts her on the radar for when the squad is announced in May.

"I actually didn't know she [Yapp] was there until after the game, but I'm very happy that we gave the performance that we did in front of her," said Tuipulotu.

"It's probably number one on my goal list right now, to perform the best I can to put my hand up for a spot on that team."

One year until first women's Lions Test - will it be a success?

Wales deliver performance of serious promise

Tuipulotu, 23, exploded onto the international scene in the 2023 Six Nations, where she earned her "prop idol" nickname.

But injuries and potentially a lack of confidence amid Wales' slump in form never saw her reach the heights of her early promise.

But fans saw the Tuipulotu of old on Friday, with former Wales centre Jonathan Davies calling her performance "world class" during punditry.

Tuipulotu, who joined Harlequins from Gloucester-Hartpury in the summer, credits the six weeks of pre-season for getting her back to her best shape.

"This is probably the best place where I could be physically," she said.

"In the last year I've come back from injury, but I haven't played the rugby that I wanted to play, so I'm happy with how Friday went."

Saturday, 26 September at 15:00 BST

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

Wales' attention now turns to USA, who they face at Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday (15:00 BST).

USA pulled off a stunning comeback victory against Ireland on Sunday, and are now up to sixth in the world, while Wales have risen two places to 11th.

"We'll go into this game confident," said Tuipulotu.

"We're going into this game with a win in hand, but to back it up even more will just give us that fire in our bellies to go out and perform.

"If we just carry on playing the way we do and improve every week, then hopefully we get the crowd there too."

title: Scotland's Scott promoted to PGA Tour with Ohio win
description: Scotland's Sandy Scott puts a career-threatening wrist injury behind him to earn promotion to the main PGA Tour for the first time after winning the Nationwide Children's Hospital Championship in Columbus, Ohio.
fullText:
Scotland's Sandy Scott has put a career-threatening wrist injury behind him to earn promotion to the main PGA Tour for the first time by winning the Nationwide Children's Hospital Championship in Columbus, Ohio.

The 28-year-old's one-stroke victory on Sunday was his first on the Korn Ferry Tour and lifted him to second spot on the development tour's points list.

It came a week after he finished runner-up at the Simmons Bank Open for the Snedeker Foundation in Franklin, Tennessee.

The native of Inverness needed two surgeries after tearing ligaments in his right wrist in 2019 and admitted: "I was in some really low times and didn't know if I'd ever play golf again."

MacIntyre finishes equal 10th as Spaun wins PGA Championship

Scott battled back from that but withdrew from this season's BMW Charity Pro-Am and missed two months of the season after the wrist flared up again.

"It was just getting progressively worse," he told the Golf Channel. "Every day, it was harder to warm up and I was getting a bit more sharp pain.

"With having a history of having a wrist injury, I've kind of gone through the waves of being unsure about what golf's going to look like for me in the future.

"When I did come back from it in college, I had this overwhelming sense of perspective that I'm just happy to be out here competing, fulfilling this dream that I've always had of playing golf professionally. To be able to play well has been a bonus."

Scott started his latest event in 13th place on the tour, but he birdied two of his final three holes to close with a six-under 65 on the Scarlet Course at Ohio State University Golf Club to post 18-under 266 and break the 72-hole tournament record, edging out American John Marshall Butler for the win.

He becomes the seventh player - and first European - to have qualified for the main tour during the 2027 season.

Scott had finished 55th in his rookie season on the development tour last year but will next year return to a PGA Tour event for the first time since the 2020 US Open at Winged Foot Golf Club, when he qualified by finishing sixth in the World Amateur Golf Ranking.

"It's been a weird journey and I'm just so happy," he said.

title: Ex-Birmingham winger Graham in hospital after serious accident
description: Former Birmingham winger Jordan Graham is in hospital after being involved in a "serious road traffic accident".
fullText:
Former Birmingham City winger Jordan Graham is in hospital after being involved in a "serious road traffic accident".

A statement issued by the Professional Footballers' Association, external (PFA), on behalf of Graham's family, said the 31-year-old was "receiving specialist treatment" after the incident earlier this month.

Graham played 49 times in the Championship for Birmingham between 2021 and 2023 after joining from Gillingham.

An Aston Villa academy product, he also played 17 times for Wolves and had loan spells with Ipswich Town, Bradford City, Oxford United and Fulham.

In total, he has made 188 career appearances but has not played since leaving Leyton Orient in 2025.

"His family are incredibly grateful for the care he is receiving," the PFA statement added.

"They respectfully ask for privacy and that people refrain from contacting them directly while they focus entirely on Jordan and his recovery.

"Further information will only be provided when appropriate."

A statement from Gillingham said: "Everyone at the club is thinking of Jordan and his family at this time.

"We wish him a full and swift recovery."

Orient added: "We're all with you JG."

title: Bred for success - why Backstedt can hit cycling's peaks
description: Zoe Backstedt won world time trial silver in Montreal aged just 21 and the multiple junior world champion plans to win much more.
fullText:
The beaming smile fits the remarkable achievement. The words offer up the tinge of regret from a potential cycling great in the making.

"I have to say I'm happy, but at the same time of course I also came here for a gold medal," said Zoe Backstedt, shortly after collecting time trial silver at cycling's Road World Championships in Montreal.

The response also demonstrates both a youthful exuberance and a maturity not all can muster, even well beyond Backstedt's 21 years.

"To be still 21, my first elite and still eligible for the under-23s, to be second is really incredible and I've had a smile on my face since the second I crossed the line. It's been a really cool day," she added.

But then the Welsh talent - who will celebrate her 22nd birthday later this week - has already been winning for years, having been raised from a successful cycling family and, many have long agreed, destined for the very top of the sport.

GB's Backstedt wins world time-trial silver

Women's cycling could be unstoppable - Backstedt

Welsh teenager follows lead of Olympic great Kenny

Backstedt carries a famous name around with her.

Her father Magnus won the famous cobbled Paris-Roubaix one-day race and a stage of the Tour de France during a lengthy career as a professional, before moving into coaching and broadcasting.

Her mother Megan won the British Road Race national title, competed for Great Britain at World Championships and for Wales at the Commonwealth Games.

Her older sister Elynor is also a talented professional cyclist with back-to-back medals at the Junior Road World Championships in 2018 and 2019.

"For a long, long time I actually hated cycling," Zoe, the youngest of the family, once told the BBC.

"It took me until I was maybe 10 or 11 to enjoy it.

"At the time I was doing cycling, netball, tennis and athletics all at once. I'd go out on the bike, but I'd say to dad that I don't want to do any more than two hours. I was adamant.

"Then one day it just clicked and I thought this is what I want to do."

At 17, Backstedt became the youngest ever winner of a women's elite cycling race in Belgium, with a cyclo-cross win in Essen.

Having claimed the Junior World Road Race gold in Flanders in 2021, a year down the line she not only retained her title but also added the time-trial crown.

In 2025, still only 20 and riding her first world under-23 time trial, she demolished the field, finishing one minute 51 seconds ahead of her nearest rival on a hilly course in Rwanda.

Again, her post-race words gave a deep insight into her sporting determination.

"It's brutal climbing here, but I really like it," she said after conquering a course which included a punishing cobbled incline.

It has not all been plain sailing. In 2024, sickness meant she missed out on a chance to ride at the Paris Olympics.

Her 2025 cyclo-cross season was interrupted by a broken hand and wrist, which kept her out of racing until January of this year, when she returned with seventh in the women's elite race at the Cyclo-Cross World Championships in Hulst, Netherlands.

When you are as determined - and talented - as Zoe Backstedt, such setbacks can be merely launching pads for even better to come.

Back on the road in June, she took her ninth professional victory - winning a sprint stage at the Tour de Suisse Femmes.

Over the next 10 days she doubled up at the British Road Championships - first successfully defending her elite time-trial crown before winning her first British road race title with another emphatic victory in Aberystwyth.

In July, she retained the Baloise Ladies Tour title, a year after becoming the youngest winner of the race.

She rode the Tour de France Femmes for the first time in August - a "goosebumps" moment, she told the BBC - finishing a creditable fourth in the time-trial stage.

And now, in September - having declined the opportunity to defend her U23 title - she finished second to 35-year-old Swiss Marlen Reusser who retained her elite world time trial crown in Canada.

"I'm over the moon with my performance," Backstedt told the BBC after a few hours to reflect on her ride.

"It was really a crazy long time trial so to take home the silver medal, I'm super proud of that."

Backstedt is not finished yet either in Montreal. On Saturday, 26 September she will line up as one of the leaders for Great Britain in the road race.

"It's going to be a hard course, that's for sure," said Backstedt.

"But myself and Lauren Dixon will be the leaders and I think with the team that we've got coming, we will make it a really hard race."

A hard race, just the way she likes it.

She has no intention of making life easier by concentrating on one cycling discipline.

"I would like to continue across them all," Backstedt said.

"I think it's something I really enjoy.

"Time-trialling, road, cyclocross, they're all three disciplines that I really love doing and I love racing so I can't really say if I would choose one or the other.

"I think putting all of them in there and doing a lot of work for all of them is what makes me stronger by the end of the season as well, so I will continue to race all of them."

And, almost certainly, Backstedt will continue to win more medals too.

title: Hawkins among five World Cup winners in England squad
description: Rob Hawkins is among five Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup winners who will attempt to help England defend the trophy in Australia this autumn.
fullText:
Rob Hawkins is among five Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup winners who will attempt to help England defend the trophy in Australia this autumn.

Hawkins, Wheelchair Super League's top try-scorer this season with 70, scored four tries as Halifax Panthers completed a domestic treble by beating Leeds Rhinos to win Sunday's Grand Final.

He is joined in England's 10-player final World Cup squad by club-mates Jack Brown - who scored six tries in that final - and Finlay O'Neill.

Both Hawkins and Brown were part of the England squad who defeated France dramatically at Manchester Central in November 2022 to win the World Cup.

So too was Lewis King, who will captain England down under, plus King's London Roosters club-mate Joe Coyd and Leeds Rhinos' Nathan Collins.

Collins will be joined in the England squad by Leeds team-mate Tristan Norfolk, Roosters' Mason Billington and the Sheffield Eagles pair of Luis Domingos and Chris Haynes.

England face Wales on Friday, 30 October (04:30 GMT) in their opening match at the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup - which will be staged alongside the men's and women's tournaments.

They then face the USA on Tuesday, 3 November (07:30 GMT) and Ireland on Friday, 6 November (06:00 GMT), aiming to secure a spot in the following Tuesday's semi-finals.

The wheelchair tournament will be staged at the Wollongong Entertainment Centre, with the final on Friday, 13 November (08:30 GMT).

England head coach Tom Coyd - who led the side to their World Cup success in Manchester four years ago - said: "Every player understands what it means to wear the England shirt and the responsibility that comes with it.

"Yesterday's brilliant Wheelchair Super League Grand Final was a testament to the special community that we are privileged to represent on the world stage."

England's wheelchair squad will fly out to Australia on 22 October.

England squad: Mason Billington (London Roosters), Jack Brown (Halifax Panthers), Nathan Collins (Leeds Rhinos), Joe Coyd (London Roosters), Luis Domingos (Sheffield Eagles), Rob Hawkins (Halifax Panthers), Chris Haynes (Sheffield Eagles), Lewis King (London Roosters), Tristan Norfolk (Leeds Rhinos), Finlay O'Neill (Halifax Panthers).

title: Wales will have no fear in Portugal - James
description: Jordan James insists depleted Wales will not be overawed against "the best players in the world" in their Nations League A opener against Portugal on Thursday.
fullText:
Jordan James insists depleted Wales will not be overawed when they line up against "the best players in the world" in their Nations League A opener against Portugal on Thursday.

A Wales squad already missing the likes of Joe Rodon and Dylan Lawlor has been hit by the withdrawals of Karl Darlow, Nathan Broadhead and star man Harry Wilson.

Having returned to the top tier of the Nations League by winning their League B group in 2024, Wales begin what looks like being a demanding campaign as they meet a star-studded Portuguese side in Lisbon.

Portugal can call on a string of star names including Ruben Dias, Joao Cancelo, Nuno Mendes, Vitinha, Joao Neves and Bruno Fernandes, not to mention 41-year-old Cristiano Ronaldo.

But Wolverhampton Wanderers midfielder James says Wales will have "no fear" as they go in search of a first win since last November's World Cup qualifying triumph against North Macedonia.

"Obviously they're the best players in the world at the end of the day, you can't really sugarcoat it," James said.

Thursday, 24 September, 19:45 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"They've got Champions League winners, they've got these kinds of things.

"I think we're always underdogs. We're used to it, so hopefully we can use that to benefit ourselves.

"You can't count us out. We've got a puncher's chance at the end of the day and we're going there to sort of cause an upset."

James is likely to be in direct competition with a Portuguese midfield regarded by some as the best in world football.

In Portugal's most recent game, the 1-0 defeat by Spain in the round of 16 at this summer's World Cup, Paris St-Germain duo Neves and Vitinha lined up at the base of midfield with Manchester United captain Fernandes in front of them.

But 21-cap James has faced similar challenges before in his young career, having memorably produced a stellar performance when Wales beat a Croatia team featuring a midfield three of Luka Modric, Marcelo Brozovic and Mateo Kovacic in October 2023.

"I've still got Kovacic's shirt on the game up in my room," said James, who was 19 at the time of the Croatia triumph.

"That was a really proud moment for me at such a young age to be able to compete against the best.

"It was a really proud moment and hopefully there will be many, many more."

James says he does not get nervous about facing star names – although he did feel "a bit star-struck" when he lined up for Leicester City against Frank Lampard's Coventry City last season because the former England midfielder is his idol.

James, who was born 11 months after Ronaldo joined Manchester United the first time in 2003, describes the prospect of facing the former Real Madrid forward as "a bit mad".

He says Ronaldo's career – which has so far included 146 international goals over 23 years – is a result of superhuman qualities.

"We're all trying to achieve the same thing, to be the best player in the world," James said.

"But you get those sort of aliens in a way that don't seem human. You look at the Messis, the Neymars, the Ronaldos - they've just got that extra little quality where in big moments they turn up and can do it again and again and again.

"I think that's the main thing. The longevity of how they're able to do it is unbelievable."

title: Carse needs time away, says 'good mate' Brook
description: England white-ball captain Harry Brook says his "very good mate" Brydon Carse needs time away from international cricket.
fullText:
England white-ball captain Harry Brook said his "very good mate" Brydon Carse needs time away from international cricket.

Pace bowler Carse was arrested then de-arrested on a night out in Derby in August.

On Friday, Derbyshire Police confirmed an investigation into an alleged assault has ended, with no further action taken.

Carse now faces an investigation by the Cricket Regulator.

Though he remains available for England selection, he has not been chosen in any format of the game since the incident.

Batter Brook is a close friend of the Durham seamer and the pair share an agent.

"I'm very good mates with Carsey," Brook told BBC Sport.

"I've spoken a lot with him. I think he just needs time away from the international scene.

"He's working on a few things behind the scenes and hopefully he'll be ready at some point in the future."

Brook has endured his own tough period off the field – in October last year he was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington on the eve of a one-day international against New Zealand.

The 27-year-old said he would be able to pass on his experience of dealing with controversy.

Though Carse, 31, is available for England selection, the England and Wales Cricket Board has said he will "take time" to "work through the issues that led to the Derby incident".

White-ball head coach Brendon McCullum said Carse needs to "get his house order" before he can play for England again.

At the weekend, new Test coach Stephen Fleming discussed the "standards" England players must meet.

Before Tuesday's first one-day international against Sri Lanka at Chester-le-Street, Brook said there will eventually be a "debate" over the prospects of Carse receiving a recall.

"He's a very good cricketer, we all know that," said Brook.

"He's been bowling extremely well for Durham. When his time for selection is up, that will be a debate."

Leg-spinner Adil Rashid will miss the opener to the three-match series against Sri Lanka because of a hand injury.

With Jacob Bethell already absent following knee surgery, Tom Banton will open the batting.

England hammered the tourists 3-0 in a one-sided T20 series last week. Brook's team have been superb in the shortest format, winning 23 of their past 26 completed internationals.

But the next global tournament is the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa in October and November 2027, and Brook said that 50-over cricket will now be given priority.

"Naturally it does, with the World Cup being next year," said Brook.

"That's not saying we're taking anything away from T20 cricket at all, because we're absolutely flying in that format at the minute.

"With the World Cup being just around the corner, and now we've solidified qualification, we can really start to home in on what the squad and XI is."

Tuesday's game in Durham will be England's first ODI since adding Kevin Pietersen to their backroom staff.

Former England batter Pietersen has been recruited as a mentor for the build-up to the 50-over World Cup. On Monday, he began the hosts' training with a session on how to play spin bowling.

Brook's side are now on a diet of white-ball cricket up to the Test tour of South Africa in December.

Before then, and following the conclusion of the series against Sri Lanka on Sunday, they travel to Pakistan in October for a one-day tri-series that also includes the Sri Lankans.

In November, England are in Australia for three ODIs and five T20s against their Ashes rivals.

The T20 series in Australia finishes a week before England's sole warm-up game in South Africa.

Because of the tight turnaround, some of the multi-format fast bowlers are likely to be rested for the T20s in Australia, meaning a break for the likes of Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue, Gus Atkinson and possibly Sonny Baker.

The squads for the tours of Pakistan and Australia are set to be named next week, along with a new batch of central contracts. The group to tour South Africa for Fleming's first series in charge will come in October.

Meanwhile, Jonathan Trott has been named England Lions head coach for their winter tours of West Indies, South Africa and Sri Lanka.

Former England batter Trott's four-year spell in charge of Afghanistan came to an end in February.

A contender for the England Test job before Fleming was appointed in July, Trott replaces Andrew Flintoff, who stepped down in August.

title: How is Scotland squad shaping up for Pocognoli debut?
description: Sebastien Pocognoli's faces his first test as Scotland head coach against Slovenia on Saturday, but how are his squad shaping up for his debut?
fullText:
Sometimes luck can be the difference between success and failure as a manager and Sebastien Pocognoli appears to have it with him for his first Scotland squad - at least before a ball is kicked.

Scott McTominay was obviously a notable miss from the new head coach's original selection, the 29-year-old Napoli midfielder having to undergo what he described as minor heart surgery that should only keep him sidelined for a few weeks.

Rangers' Lawrence Shankland and Torino's Che Adams are also absentees from the frontline options through injury.

But, of the 28 players named in Pocognoli's extended squad for Scotland's opening four Nations League fixtures, none have so far pulled out through injury.

So how are they shaping up after their latest round of club games?

Pocognoli Facetime helps Miller over summer of discontent

Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate

Scottish Football Podcast: Belief is back for Rangers as Celtic in turmoil

The goalkeeping position was a problem for some time under predecessor Steve Clarke, exacerbated by 84-cap Craig Gordon coming to the end of his career and with playing time often limited for the alternatives.

But current first-choice Angus Gunn is now a regular starter with San Jose Earthquakes after his summer switch from Nottingham Forest.

Scott Bain is also performing well for Falkirk, while Jon McCracken has helped Bradford City to the top of League One after his move from Dundee, making Rangers' Liam Kelly the only goalkeeper not playing for his club.

The absence of Shankland and Adams gave Pocognoli the opportunity to bring in some fresh blood among the forwards, and the recalled Oli McBurnie continues to start for Hull City on their return to the Premier League.

Meanwhile, Robbie Ure was back in the starting line-up for new club Sevilla as they lost 3-1 to La Liga leaders Barcelona on Saturday, while James Wilson has cemented a first-team place since returning to Heart of Midlothian from his loan to Tottenham Hotspur.

In saying that, striker Kieron Bowie and wingers Findlay Curtis and Ben Gannon-Doak had to make do with being substitutes over the weekend for Sassuolo, Rangers and Bournemouth respectively.

While 20-year-old Gannon-Doak's continued lack of minutes is not ideal considering he has proved to be a key provider of pace to Scotland's play, club-mate Ryan Christie will have received a boost by being handed only his second start of the season, albeit the midfielder came off after 75 minutes of a 1-0 home defeat by Liverpool.

Indeed, all seven of Pocognoli's central midfield options started at the weekend.

That includes Lennon Miller in Udinese's 1-0 home defeat by Cagliari. Also in Serie A, Billy Gilmour scored only his second senior goal with a fine strike in Napoli's 1-1 draw at Fiorentina, as well as being named man of the match.

Meanwhile, Lewis Ferguson is back starting every game as Bologna captain, including their 1-1 draw with Torino.

For visitors Torino, Nathan Patterson made his second appearance as a substitute since his loan move from Everton as right-back continues to be a problem area for Scotland.

Aaron Hickey also had to make do with coming off the bench in Brentford's fine 3-0 win over Chelsea.

Colby Donovan did start again for Celtic, albeit as the Scottish champions suffered a third straight defeat, while all three left-backs - Donovan's club-mate Kieran Tierney, Tottenham Hotspur's Andy Robertson and Sassuolo's Josh Doig suffered losses after starting.

Only Scott McKenna - an unused sub as Croatian league leaders Dinamo Zagreb beat Lokomotiva - did not play in his club side's latest game among Pocognoli's defensive options.

With Gilmour the only weekend goalscorer and Robertson and Aston Villa midfielder John McGinn providing an assist each in Spurs' 3-2 defeat, Pocognoli could look to that experienced trio to provide the creative spark for the Nations League matches starting away to Slovenia on Saturday.

title: Tesla faces major trial for alleged bias against Black workers after years of lawsuits
description:
A California agency's lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination at its flagship assembly plant is set to go to trial on Monday, one of a ‌series of similar lawsuits being faced by the electric vehicle maker. 
   Lawyers for Tesla and the California ‌Civil Rights Department will square off in Oakland before state Superior Court Judge Peter Borkon, who has scheduled the trial to run until October ​30. 
   In the lawsuit filed in 2022, the California Civil Rights Department claims Black workers at Tesla's Fremont, California plant were subjected to pervasive harassment by other employees, including racial slurs and graffiti, and Tesla failed to prevent or stop it. Tesla is also accused of paying Black workers less than others and depriving them of opportunities for promotions. 
   Tesla and ‌its lawyers did not respond to requests ⁠for comment.
fullText:
Sept 21 (Reuters) - A California agency's lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination at its flagship assembly plant is set to go to trial on Monday, one of a ‌series of similar lawsuits being faced by the electric vehicle maker.

Lawyers for Tesla and the California ‌Civil Rights Department will square off in Oakland before state Superior Court Judge Peter Borkon, who has scheduled the trial to run until October ​30.

In the lawsuit filed in 2022, the California Civil Rights Department claims Black workers at Tesla's Fremont, California plant were subjected to pervasive harassment by other employees, including racial slurs and graffiti, and Tesla failed to prevent or stop it. Tesla is also accused of paying Black workers less than others and depriving them of opportunities for promotions.

Tesla and ‌its lawyers did not respond to requests ⁠for comment. The company has denied wrongdoing and said that it does not tolerate discrimination and has fired workers found to have engaged in misconduct.

The California Civil Rights Department's director, ⁠Kevin Kish, in a statement said the agency looked forward to holding Tesla accountable.

Tesla's high profile and the thousands of workers involved in the case make it among the most significant involving employment discrimination claims against a major US company to ​go ​to trial in recent years.

Borkon has scheduled ​a bench trial, meaning that he and not ‌a jury will decide whether Tesla is liable for violations of California civil rights laws.

Unlike federal law, the California law barring workplace discrimination does not cap the damages a court can award to affected workers, and Tesla could be on the hook for many millions of dollars if it loses the case.

Tesla has for the last decade been dogged by claims that it fostered a climate at the Fremont plant and other facilities that was extremely ‌hostile to Black workers. The company is also facing a lawsuit ​from the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission alleging racial harassment, and ​dozens of lawsuits by individual workers making similar ​claims.

The claims in the Civil Rights Department's lawsuit are broader and include allegations that the ‌Fremont plant was racially segregated, with Black workers ​assigned to the lowest-paying and ​least desirable jobs.

Borkon ruled in a separate lawsuit last year that more than 6,000 Black workers could not sue Tesla as a class, reversing an earlier decision and handing a major victory to the company.

title: How will clubs train during three-week international break?
description: BBC Sport looks at how clubs are planning to deal with the extended three-week international break.
fullText:
The first international break of the season is under way - and this one is longer than fans will have become accustomed to.

For the first time, the Premier League and the Championship will come to a halt for three weeks rather than the usual two.

Football fans tend not to love international breaks, but this change has been done with good intentions.

It merges the four games played in the old September and October breaks into one slot.

So the domestic game stops for three weeks, rather than four weeks across two windows. Club football is actually getting a week back.

But for players not on international duty, three weeks is a long time for finely tuned athletes not to play competitively.

So how are clubs going to deal with this change?

Here's how different teams plan to balance the international break.

Most squads in the Premier League these days are packed with international players, and Brentford are no different.

Most of the Bees' squad are away, with about 12 players - including Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago - left at their training facility, including five who are coming back from injury.

Brentford have a longer break than almost every other team, given they hosted Chelsea on Friday evening.

Boss Keith Andrews has given his first-team players a week off with individual training programmes to follow. Those players will not have restrictions on leaving the country, but it is unlikely long-haul flights would be sanctioned.

The squad will reconvene on Saturday, 26 September to begin training again, before playing a behind-closed-doors game against another English club on the weekend of 3 October.

That friendly could potentially give the likes of Nathan Collins and Sepp van den Berg a chance to return to action, with the rest of the squad made up of under-21 players.

The second international break will look very different, with the Bees playing Brighton on Sunday, 8 November and back in action against Everton on Saturday, 21 November.

Players may be given the odd day off, but in general it will be a normal training programme with no friendly before the usual preparation for the fixture against the Toffees.

Liverpool, meanwhile, will carry on training with the small number of players that remain, with a few days off.

Manager Andoni Iraola says he will be left with "no more than three days probably to prepare" for the home game with Manchester City on 11 October.

Aston Villa have a very different international break planned.

Unai Emery will return to former club Sevilla, where he won the Europa League three times on the bounce.

Sevilla and Villa will face off in the 15th edition of the Antonio Puerta Trophy on Friday, 2 October.

The game is played in memory of the 22-year-old Sevilla wing-back, who died on 28 August 2007 after having multiple cardiac arrests on the pitch during a La Liga game against Getafe.

While Premier League teams see their squads decimated by international call-ups, it is not quite as dramatic in the Championship.

Many clubs will only have a handful, such as Blackburn Rovers with just four call-ups.

For Rovers boss Tony Mowbray this break will be a positive for a couple of reasons.

Mowbray has had to contend with an injury crisis in the early part of the season, with more than 10 players ruled out in the opening weeks.

The break gives Rovers the chance to ease some of those players back into action, such as Gady Beyuku and Moussa Baradji who recently made their comebacks, and others close to a return like Scott Wharton.

After the trip to Portsmouth on Saturday, Rovers headed back to Lancashire and will have a few days on the training ground this week.

After such a busy start to the campaign, with league fixtures and the Carabao Cup, it also gives Mowbray - who returned to the club in the summer - a chance to properly work with his players.

But it will not all be training.

Mowbray intends to give the players a few days off from the end of the week. Players such as Yuri Ribeiro will be able to return home to Portugal, if they so wish.

The cycle will then be repeated the following week, training the first half with a short break over the weekend. Then for week three, it is back to the usual pre-match routine before the home game against Cardiff.

Mowbray is also looking to find a Premier League or League One team to play in a behind-closed-doors friendly.

It will help those returning from injury to get minutes in the bank, and keep other members of the squad ticking over.

In the two-week break in November, players may still get a short spell off while matches are more likely to be in-house affairs with teams made up of senior and under-21 players.

The three-week international break might have posed a unique situation for a couple of clubs, whereby they could have a full squad and no games to play.

League One carries on playing unless clubs get three call-ups which meet the EFL's criteria, then a postponement can be requested.

Only four of the 12 matches have survived on each of the two weekends.

Yet many clubs prepared in advance by scheduling Football League Trophy fixtures during these three weeks.

Clubs tend to rotate in this competition anyway, so the games still go ahead even if league games are postponed.

Twelve teams will play two trophy ties, with 10 clubs playing once.

That left just Leyton Orient and Reading at risk at not having a game to play. Both have only had one league match called off, so will not have all three weeks vacant.

title: Hunter faces manslaughter charge after mistaking woman for deer, police say
description:
A 74-year-old hunter has been arrested and charged in a homicide investigation in which police allege he fatally shot a woman in Delaware whom he allegedly mistook for a deer.
Walter Moorhead of Salisbury, Maryland, was charged with manslaughter and related crimes after allegedly shooting the woman while hunting Friday evening in a field near Ellendale, Delaware, according to the Delaware State Police.
"The preliminary investigation revealed that the victim was walking through the field with a man and two children while Moorhead was hunting deer from a ground blind. Moorhead believed he saw a deer and fired his rifle, striking the victim," the Delaware State Police said in a statement.
Delaware State Police - PHOTO: Walter Moorhead, a 74-year-old hunter from Salisbury, Maryland, was charged with felony manslaughter, September 18, 2026, in the fatal shooting in Delaware of a woman he mistook for a deer, according to the Delaware State Police.
fullText:
The victim was identified by police as 39-year-old Santos Maria Chilel Soto.

A 74-year-old hunter has been arrested and charged in a homicide investigation in which police allege he fatally shot a woman in Delaware whom he allegedly mistook for a deer.

Walter Moorhead of Salisbury, Maryland, was charged with manslaughter and related crimes after allegedly shooting the woman while hunting Friday evening in a field near Ellendale, Delaware, according to the Delaware State Police.

"The preliminary investigation revealed that the victim was walking through the field with a man and two children while Moorhead was hunting deer from a ground blind. Moorhead believed he saw a deer and fired his rifle, striking the victim," the Delaware State Police said in a statement.

The victim was identified Sunday as 39-year-old Santos Maria Chilel Soto of Georgetown, Delaware, according to the state police.

The incident unfolded around 7:40 p.m. on Friday, according to the state police, who said troopers who were called to the scene provided lifesaving medical care to the victim, who was later pronounced dead at a hospital.

Troopers took Moorhead into custody after a preliminary investigation "determined that he had fired the shot that struck the victim," according to the state police.

In addition to the charge of felony manslaughter, Moorhead is facing three counts of first-degree reckless endangerment, as well as a count of possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, state police said.

Moorhead was arraigned by the Justice of the Peace Court and released after posting a $43,000 cash bond, according to the state police.

Moorhead did not immediately return a call from ABC News on Sunday seeking comment at a phone number listed for him. It was unclear if he had hired an attorney.

The Delaware State Police said the shooting remains under investigation and asked anyone with information about the incident to call its homicide unit.

title: Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate
description: Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is being investigated over an issue with his Covid-19 vaccination certificate.
fullText:
Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is under investigation by Swiss prosecutors over allegations he obtained a forged Covid-19 vaccination certificate.

The 33-year-old is alleged to have obtained the certificate in 2022, when it was a requirement in Switzerland for some travel abroad.

The public prosecutor's office of the city of Lucerne confirmed the investigation was under way to determine whether any criminal behaviour took place in obtaining a "false or forged" certificate.

The Sunderland midfielder, who was playing for Arsenal at the time, posted a statement on social media on Monday saying he had a "mistrust" towards the vaccine and had been "influenced by worries and uncertainty".

He said: "In this troubled state of mind I acquired a vaccine certificate, instead of clarifying my unanswered questions in the proper way.

"Today I see clearly, that this way was not correct. It was a mistake. I'm sorry.

"I take responsibility for this decision, will engage with the process of establishing the facts and fully co-operate with the relevant authorities."

The Swiss office of public health confirmed that while there was never a general legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel, meaning that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one.

These measures in Switzerland were in place until spring 2022. After that point, Covid-19 certificates continued to be issued, primarily to enable members of the public to meet entry requirements when travelling abroad.

It is unclear what punishments Xhaka could face, but in 2023 the then Switzerland men's ice hockey coach Patrick Fischer was found guilty of using a fake Covid-19 certificate to work at the 2022 Winter Olympics ‌in Beijing.

Fischer was fined 38,000 Swiss francs by a criminal court. In April this year, he was sacked from the Switzerland job and earlier this month, he was banned for four years by the International Ice Hockey Federation.

The Swiss Football Association said Xhaka, the country's record appearance holder with 152 caps, had withdrawn from the Swiss camp for their upcoming Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia following his statement.

It added the decision to withdraw had been made jointly by the player and management and that they would discuss Xhaka's future with the team after the international window.

Switzerland have away fixtures against North Macedonia and Scotland on 26 and 29 September, before facing Slovenia and North Macedonia at home in early October.

Sunderland boss Regis le Bris refused to comment on the allegations following the Black Cats' defeat at Manchester City on Sunday.

"It is not my area to speak about those problems or situations," he said. "My area is football. About football, he is really good."

Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year, where they were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual runners-up Argentina.

title: Was Neville right to call out Man Utd for a 'lack of effort'?
description: Was Gary Neville right to call out Manchester United for a "lack of effort" in their 1-1 draw at Fulham on Sunday?
fullText:
"I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic."

Gary Neville did not hold back in his criticism of the Manchester United's performance during Sky Sports' coverage of Sunday's 1-1 draw at Fulham.

The players had just laboured through the opening period of the second half, culminating in a Lisandro Martinez own goal gifting the home side the lead.

"I've never seen such a lack of effort," Neville added. "What must Michael Carrick be thinking?"

Neville played 602 games for United over a 19-year career, winning everything the club game had to offer. So his criticism comes from a qualified position.

This season's out-of-possession stats would appear to back it up too, with the Red Devils ranking 16th for distance covered, and 17th for total number of sprints.

But does that tell the whole story?

How did United play under Carrick when they were winning games towards the end of last season?

And, as Neville makes the headlines, what does this say about his influence in the media around Manchester United?

United's dismal running and sprinting stats made for stark reading in the wake of Neville's criticism.

After all, the former right-back had directly questioned a lack of effort, and referred to the players as "mannequins".

He said United - and Fulham - were walking too much during the game.

In the Premier League this season only four teams have covered less distance than the Red Devils, and just three teams have produced fewer sprints.

It comes alongside United's joint-worst start to a Premier League season, with four points from five games.

So is this down to the running and the effort?

Let's take a look at the second half of last season, after Carrick had been appointed as manager.

Between 17 January and the end of the season, United picked up more points than any other team - 39 points from 17 games.

Yet only four teams ran less than United, and only two clubs had fewer sprints.

There is no material difference in the running stats, but United were returning 2.29 points per game compared to the 0.8 this season.

Something is clearly different, but it does not appear to be linked to this particular stat because barely anything has changed - apart from the results. Maybe this United squad simply does not have runners.

Then there is the comparison to rival teams.

Manchester City have won all five Premier League matches, but have covered less distance than United. Enzo Maresca's squad have also recorded the lowest number of sprints in the division.

Brighton, one of the most exciting teams in the league this season and the top goalscorers, are one place above United for sprints.

Maybe United's problem is tactical rather than a simple case of not running enough?

Neville setting the media agenda when it comes to United is not a new thing.

The former England international has called out the team's shortcomings on many occasions.

Look back to December 2021, and a poor first-half performance against a struggling Newcastle side which saw Ralf Rangnick's side trail 1-0 at the break.

"They're a bunch of whinge-bags," Neville said at half-time on Sky Sports. "I'll not go into names but they're whinging at each other, arms up in the air complaining about everything.

"There's no pressing, no urgency, the basics of the game."

Edinson Cavani rescued a point at St James Park, but Neville's comments had already made the headlines.

You only need to look at how the post-match coverage went after the Fulham draw.

Neville's remarks were put to Carrick at full-time. The United manager said fitness levels of his players were not an issue.

"Neville: That was the worst ever", read the back page of Monday's Daily Telegraph.

"15 minutes of shame", was the lead for the sports section of the Daily Star.

"United boss keeps calm after Neville Ful blast," said the Daily Express.

It was picked up across online media, and discussed at length on radio talk shows - including across the BBC, as evidenced by this piece.

When Neville criticises his former club, it carries weight.

In January, with Ruben Amorim under pressure for poor results, the Portuguese said that "if people cannot handle the Gary Nevilles and the criticisms of everything, we need to change the club".

Amorim was dismissed the following day.

There always seems to be a strong influence in the media related to the dominant team of a previous era.

For example throughout the 1990s and 2000s, former Liverpool stars such as Alan Hansen, Mark Lawrenson and Phil Thompson dominated a lot of the conversation.

It stands to reason that now members of the all-conquering United squad will have a leading role in the media.

But for Neville, it is bigger than anyone apart from Gary Lineker and his Goalhanger production company.

How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls

Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief

'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict

"When does Sky wonder if they are paying a lot of money in wages to train their next competitor?"

It is a question posed by Richard Gillis, who hosts the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast.

While Neville started out in the media as a pundit with Sky Sports, the 51-year-old is now one of the biggest players in a rapidly changing industry.

After co-founding the sports entertainment production company Buzz16 in 2016, Neville launched YouTube platform 'The Overlap' in 2021.

'The Overlap' produces 'Stick to Football' - one of the UK's most popular football content channels with 2.2 billion views across all platforms in 2025.

Earlier this year it entered into a strategic partnership with radio giants Global, with the aim to create a multi-format sports media network.

Neville this summer exited Buzz16, focusing his attention on 'The Overlap', which has branched out into cricket and rugby, and secured live Bundesliga rights.

The YouTube channels of United influencer Mark Goldbridge's were recently acquired, a further sign of the influence Neville now wields in football's media industry.

Goldbridge made his name with expletive-laden rants during streamed 'watchalongs' of United matches, and his channels have around four million subscribers.

Gillis points out that Neville was attracted to the Goldbridge brand, and his United Stand podcast, because it creates noise when there is no football.

"Noise is valuable," Gillis told BBC Sport. "Man Utd generate more of it than any other club in the Premier League.

"Anger creates engagement. And from the Sky commentary box, Neville is well placed to create anger."

In a bid to ramp up its content, 'The Overlap' is believed to have targeted national newspaper journalists to come on board and cover United.

"It poses questions," Gillis says of this development.

"Currently, Neville is the story. He says something, the media reports it, the fans respond to it. A valuable loop.

"At what point does The Overlap and the United Stand (a Goldbridge channel) become the rivals of the media?"

"What is the United Stand now? A noise merchant, or a news organisation?"

To many, it probably does not matter whether Neville's comments about United's running are valid or not.

They create headlines, column inches and legitimate talking points under the Sky Sports name.

Yet Neville is himself a media mogul who also works within another organisation.

And at present, when measured by media coverage and impact, all parties are winners.
